title: "Installation"
description: "Set up your machine, create a Reactor project, and run it."
---

This page takes you from a clean Windows machine to a running
Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) app in about five minutes. You need the .NET
SDK and, for packaged apps, Developer Mode. You do not need to clone the
Reactor repository: the package is on NuGet.org, and the project templates
ship in the Windows App SDK template pack.

> **Public preview.** `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` 0.1.0-preview.18 is on
> NuGet.org. The project templates ship in the official Windows App SDK
> `dotnet new` pack (`Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK.WinUI.CSharp.Templates`).
> Broader signed distribution is tracked in
> [spec 022](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/docs/specs/022-packaging-and-distribution.md).

## Requirements [#requirements]

| Requirement | Why you need it | How to check |
|---|---|---|
| Windows 10 version 1809 (build 17763) or later, or Windows 11 | The oldest Windows version Reactor supports. | Run `winver`. |
| .NET 10 SDK or later | Reactor targets `net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0`. Single-file apps (`dotnet run app.cs`) are also a .NET 10 feature. | Run `dotnet --list-sdks` and look for a line that starts with `10.` or higher. |
| Windows App Runtime 2.x | Apps are framework-dependent by default, so they load the runtime that is installed on the machine. | Run `winget list --id Microsoft.WindowsAppRuntime.2`. |
| Developer Mode | Needed to run **packaged** apps with `dotnet run`. Unpackaged apps do not need it. | Settings → System → For developers. |
| An editor (optional) | The `dotnet` CLI is enough to build and run an app. | See [Choose an editor](#choose-an-editor). |

If the Windows App Runtime is missing, install it with
`winget install Microsoft.WindowsAppRuntime.2`. This one winget package
covers every 2.x release, so if an older 2.x runtime is installed, update it
with `winget upgrade Microsoft.WindowsAppRuntime.2`.

You do not need Visual Studio workloads or a separate Windows App SDK
install. NuGet restore brings in the Windows App SDK packages and build tools.

## Create a project [#create-a-project]

Use the `winapp` CLI, plain `dotnet new`, or a coding agent. Each way gives you
the same project.

**winapp**

The fastest way is the WinApp CLI, `winapp`.

1. **Install winapp**

    ```powershell
    winget install Microsoft.WinAppCli
    ```

2. **Create the project**

    ```powershell
    winapp new -t reactor -n MyApp
    ```

    `winapp new` installs the template pack the first time you use it, and
    offers to update a stale one. There is no separate install step and no
    version to pin. `winapp new --list` prints all templates. If you leave out
    `-t`, it asks you to pick one.

3. **Run it**

    ```powershell
    cd MyApp
    dotnet run
    ```

**dotnet new**

If you prefer plain .NET tooling, install the template pack yourself.

1. **Install the template pack**

    ```powershell
    dotnet new install Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK.WinUI.CSharp.Templates::<version>
    ```

    The pack is prerelease-only today. `dotnet new install` picks only stable
    versions unless you pin one, so the `::<version>` part is required. This is
    the step that `winapp new` does for you.

2. **Create the project**

    ```powershell
    dotnet new reactor -n MyApp
    ```

3. **Run it**

    ```powershell
    cd MyApp
    dotnet run
    ```

**With an agent**

Give this prompt to GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, or another coding agent. It
points the agent at these docs first, so it uses the real API. To give the
agent the Reactor skills too, see [Build with AI](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/build-with-ai).

**Read https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/latest/llms.txt first. Then create a Reactor app named MyApp: install the winapp CLI with `winget install Microsoft.WinAppCli` if it is missing, run `winapp new -t reactor -n MyApp`, and start the app with `dotnet run` from the MyApp folder. Fix any build errors before you stop.**

> Read https://microsoft.github.io/microsoft-ui-reactor/latest/llms.txt first.
> Then create a Reactor app named MyApp: install the winapp CLI with
> `winget install Microsoft.WinAppCli` if it is missing, run
> `winapp new -t reactor -n MyApp`, and start the app with `dotnet run` from the

### Templates [#templates]

| Template | What you get |
|---|---|
| `reactor` | A blank app with one component. |
| `reactor-mvu` | A Model-View-Update app built on `UseReducer`. |
| `reactor-navview` | An app shell with a `NavigationView`. |
| `reactor-tabview` | An app shell with a `TabView`. |
| `reactor-singlefile` | One `.cs` file and no project. See [One file, no project](#one-file-no-project). |

The project templates set up the `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` package reference, the
WinUI target framework, MSIX packaging, and an `App.cs` that mounts one
component. There is no `App.xaml` and no `MainWindow.xaml.cs`.

> **Why a custom template?** `dotnet new console` does not produce a WinUI
> app. It builds a console target with no UI thread, no `OutputType=WinExe`,
> no Windows App SDK reference and no `[STAThread]` entry point. The
> `reactor` template sets all of these, plus the Reactor package reference,
> MSIX packaging and a backdrop-aware root component. So the first
> `dotnet run` opens a window, not a console.

### Packaged or unpackaged [#packaged-or-unpackaged]

Apps created from a project template are **packaged** (single-project MSIX) by
default. `dotnet run` registers a loose-layout package and launches the app
with full package identity, the same as F5 in Visual Studio. This needs
**Developer Mode**.

For a plain unpackaged `.exe`, add `--packaging Unpackaged` to any of the four
project templates:

```powershell
dotnet new reactor -n MyApp --packaging Unpackaged
```

`winapp new` has no matching switch, so use `dotnet new` for this. An
unpackaged app has no package identity, so `Package.Current` and `ms-appx:`
URIs are not available. [Packaging](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/packaging) explains how the two shapes
differ and how to publish each one.

## Check that it works [#check-that-it-works]

`dotnet run` builds the app and opens a window with the template's starter
component. To check the whole loop, replace the contents of `App.cs` with this
small app:

```csharp
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor;
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core;
using static Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Factories;
using Microsoft.UI.Xaml;

ReactorApp.Run<GettingStartedApp>("Getting Started");

class GettingStartedApp : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (name, setName) = UseState("World");

        return VStack(16,
            TextBlock($"Hello, {name}!").FontSize(24).Bold(),
            TextBox(name, setName, placeholderText: "Enter your name")
                .AutomationName("Name")
                .Width(250)
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

Run `dotnet run` again. You see a greeting and a text box. Type in the box,
and the greeting changes as you type:

![The hello world app: a "Hello, World!" heading above a text box that holds the name](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/getting-started/hello-world.png)

If you see this window, your setup is complete.
[Your first app](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/first-app) explains this code line by line.

## One file, no project [#one-file-no-project]

A Reactor app does not need a `.csproj`. .NET 10 runs a single `.cs` file
directly, and `#:` directives at the top of the file give the settings that a
project file would otherwise hold:

```csharp
#:package Microsoft.UI.Reactor@0.1.0-preview.18
#:package Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp@0.7.0
#:property OutputType=WinExe
#:property TargetFramework=net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0
#:property UseWinUI=true

using Microsoft.UI.Reactor;
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core;
using static Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Factories;

ReactorApp.Run<MyApp>("Hello Reactor");

class MyApp : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (count, setCount) = UseState(0);

        return VStack(
            Heading($"Count: {count}"),
            HStack(8,
                Button("-", () => setCount(count - 1)),
                Button("+", () => setCount(count + 1))
            )
        );
    }
}
```

Save it as `counter.cs` and run it:

```powershell
dotnet run counter.cs
```

That is the whole app: one file, with no scaffolding and no build output to
manage. It is the fastest way to try an idea, reproduce a bug, or paste a
complete example into an issue.

Like an app from a project template, it runs packaged.
`Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp` makes `dotnet run` create an app
manifest from the `#:property` values, register the app, and launch it with
package identity. This needs **Developer Mode**. If you have the
[winapp CLI](https://github.com/microsoft/winappCli) 0.7.0 or later,
`winapp run counter.cs` does the same.

`Microsoft.UI.Reactor` brings in the Windows App SDK, just as in the
[minimal `.csproj`](#minimal-project-setup). The other directives are all
required:

| Directive | Why it is required |
|---|---|
| `Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp` | Lets `dotnet run` package the app. It carries its own copy of the winapp CLI, so you do not need to install that. Without it, `dotnet run` cannot package the app, and the app fails at startup with `COMException … REGDB_E_CLASSNOTREG`. That error does not mention the missing package. To avoid it without this package, run the app unpackaged (see below). |
| `OutputType=WinExe` | Links the app for the Windows GUI subsystem. Without it the build still succeeds, but the `.exe` is a console program, so Windows opens a console window next to your UI for as long as the app runs. |
| `TargetFramework=net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0` | Reactor ships for `net10.0-windows10.0.22621`. A lower Windows version compiles against nothing, and you get `CS0234: the namespace 'Reactor' does not exist`, as if the package were missing. |
| `UseWinUI=true` | Brings in the WinUI build targets. |

You do not have to type the header. `dotnet new reactor-singlefile -n Counter`
creates `Counter/Counter.cs` with the same five directives and a starter
component. Run `dotnet run Counter.cs` from that folder to launch it. The
template's pins differ from the block above: it targets a newer Windows SDK
(`windows10.0.26100.0`) and lets the `Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp`
version float (`@*`). Both headers work.

### Running it unpackaged [#running-it-unpackaged]

`WindowsPackageType` decides whether the app runs packaged. `dotnet run` and
`winapp run` both follow it. To run the app as a plain `.exe`, declare it
unpackaged:

```csharp
#:property WindowsPackageType=None
```

An unpackaged app has no package identity, so `Package.Current` and `ms-appx:`
URIs are not available. It does not need Developer Mode.

Packaged or not, the app is framework-dependent: it uses the Windows App
Runtime that is installed on the machine. To ship the runtime with the app
instead, add `#:property WindowsAppSDKSelfContained=true`. That mode also needs
an architecture, given with `-r win-x64` or `-r win-arm64`, because the runtime
it copies is native code built for each CPU.

## Minimal Project Setup [#minimal-project-setup]

The templates above create all of this for you. To set up a project by hand
instead, create a console project and edit the `.csproj`:

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>WinExe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0</TargetFramework>
    <UseWinUI>true</UseWinUI>
    <WindowsPackageType>None</WindowsPackageType>
    <!-- Windows App SDK needs a concrete architecture; without this an
         unqualified `dotnet build` / `dotnet run` fails with
         "WindowsAppSDKSelfContained requires a supported Windows architecture". -->
    <RuntimeIdentifier Condition="'$(RuntimeIdentifier)' == '' And ('$(Platform)' == '' Or '$(Platform)' == 'AnyCPU')">$(NETCoreSdkPortableRuntimeIdentifier)</RuntimeIdentifier>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.UI.Reactor" Version="0.1.0-preview.18" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

One package reference is enough. `Microsoft.UI.Reactor` brings in the Windows
App SDK, so add `Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK` yourself only to pin a specific WinUI
patch or to bundle the runtime with `WindowsAppSDKSelfContained`. Pin WinUI
through that full package. Do not reference `Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK.WinUI` on
its own, because it fails the Windows App SDK's version check.
[Packaging](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/packaging) covers the `<Platforms>`, ARM64 and self-contained
shapes that the project template uses.

Then replace `Program.cs` with an `App.cs` that holds a component and a
`ReactorApp.Run<T>()` call:

```csharp
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor;
using Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Core;
using static Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Factories;

ReactorApp.Run<MyApp>("My App");

class MyApp : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        return VStack(12,
            TextBlock("Hello, Reactor!").FontSize(24).Bold(),
            TextBlock("Your setup works.")
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

Run it with `dotnet run`. A window opens with the two lines of text.

## Choose an editor [#choose-an-editor]

Any editor works, because the `dotnet` CLI builds and runs every Reactor app.
These editors add more:

- **Visual Studio 2026.** Open the project and press F5 to build and debug
  it. The experimental [Visual Studio extension](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/vs-extension) adds an
  embedded live preview of a component.
- **VS Code.** The C# Dev Kit is all you need. The Reactor Preview extension
  adds a live preview panel; see the [VS Code extension](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/vs-extension#vs-code-extension).
- **Any editor and a terminal.** Run `dotnet watch` to apply code changes to
  the running app without a restart. See [Hot reload](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/hot-reload).

## Troubleshooting [#troubleshooting]

### The app fails at startup with `REGDB_E_CLASSNOTREG` [#the-app-fails-at-startup-with-regdb_e_classnotreg]

This happens with a single-file app that has no
`#:package Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp` line. Without that package,
`dotnet run` cannot package the app. Add the package line, or run the app
unpackaged with `#:property WindowsPackageType=None`. See
[One file, no project](#one-file-no-project).

### `dotnet run` cannot register or deploy a packaged app [#dotnet-run-cannot-register-or-deploy-a-packaged-app]

Packaged apps need Developer Mode. Turn it on in Settings → System → For
developers, then run `dotnet run` again. If you cannot turn it on, run the app
unpackaged (see [Packaged or unpackaged](#packaged-or-unpackaged)).

### `CS0234: the namespace 'Reactor' does not exist` [#cs0234-the-namespace-reactor-does-not-exist]

The target framework names a Windows version that is too low. Use
`net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0` or higher. This error looks like a missing
package, but the package is there.

### A console window opens next to the app [#a-console-window-opens-next-to-the-app]

`OutputType` is `Exe`, not `WinExe`. Set `<OutputType>WinExe</OutputType>` in
the `.csproj`, or `#:property OutputType=WinExe` in a single-file app.

### `WindowsAppSDKSelfContained requires a supported Windows architecture` [#windowsappsdkselfcontained-requires-a-supported-windows-architecture]

The build has no concrete architecture. The
[minimal `.csproj`](#minimal-project-setup) sets `RuntimeIdentifier` to fix
this. You can also pass the platform on the command line, for example
`dotnet build -p:Platform=x64` (or `ARM64`).

### `dotnet new` does not know `--packaging` or `reactor-singlefile` [#dotnet-new-does-not-know-packaging-or-reactor-singlefile]

The installed template pack is older than these options. Update it with
`winapp new --list --template-version latest`.

### The app starts and then reports a missing Windows App Runtime [#the-app-starts-and-then-reports-a-missing-windows-app-runtime]

The Windows App Runtime on the machine is missing or too old. Run
`winget install Microsoft.WindowsAppRuntime.2`, or `winget upgrade` if an
older 2.x runtime is installed. To avoid the machine-wide dependency, publish
the app self-contained; see [Packaging](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/packaging).

### The build fails with `MSB3073` or `PRI210` under a deep folder [#the-build-fails-with-msb3073-or-pri210-under-a-deep-folder]

The Windows App SDK's XAML and resource compilers have no long-path support.
A long project path can push `obj` and `bin` output past the 260-character
`MAX_PATH` limit. Move the project to a short path such as `C:\src\MyApp`, and
avoid OneDrive-synced folders. See
[issue #678](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/issues/678).

> **Caveat:** The template pack is prerelease-only today. `winapp new -t reactor` installs
> the newest pack and creates the project in one step. With plain `dotnet new`,
> run `dotnet new install Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK.WinUI.CSharp.Templates::<version>`
> first: without the explicit version pin, `dotnet new install` does not find the
> pack.

## Tips [#tips]

**Set the first window size.** `ReactorApp.Run<T>` takes an optional width
and height in device-independent pixels. Leave them out to let Windows choose.

```csharp
ReactorApp.Run<MyApp>("My App", width: 800, height: 600);
```

**Try an idea without a class.** For a quick test, pass a render function
instead of a component class. `ctx` gives you the same hooks a component has.

```csharp
ReactorApp.Run("Quick Test", ctx =>
{
    var (count, setCount) = ctx.UseState(0);
    return Button($"Clicked {count} times", () => setCount(count + 1));
});
```

**Keep a single-file app for bug reports.** A complete `.cs` file with the
`#:` header is the easiest repro to share in an issue.
